notes.b: Socialisation is the process by which a person learns the norms (accepted rules of behaviour), values, beliefs, language and behaviour of their society so that they can take part in it. The family is the first agent of socialisation, and school is a second, major one.
points: Formal socialisation is the planned, stated part of school: the curriculum, timetable, school rules, uniform, codes of conduct, sanctions and rewards. It teaches punctuality, respect for authority, following instructions and responsibility, because pupils must keep to these every day.

Informal socialisation is the unplanned part, called the hidden curriculum (what pupils pick up without being taught it directly): peer groups, playground rules, friendships, school routines, the school's ethos (its character and values) and the example set by teachers.

The hidden curriculum teaches sharing, taking turns, cooperation, teamwork and how to get on with others. Remember that it is not the written curriculum: rules and timetable are formal, while peer groups and playground life are informal.
School is an early and long experience of a group outside the family, so children learn to share, take turns and cooperate with others who are not relatives.
Education transmits (passes on) the culture of a society, including its language (English and Irish), customs, history, shared values, and the rights and duties of citizens.
School brings together children from different backgrounds, which helps them fit into wider society.
Through school, pupils learn to accept responsibility, follow rules and respect the rights of others.
notes.tip: For a question on education as socialisation, give formal and informal (the hidden curriculum) with an example of each, then say what is learned, such as respect, punctuality, sharing, teamwork, confidence and friendships. A typical short question asks you to name the two types of socialisation in school.

notes.b: Physical development is how the body grows stronger, more skilled and healthier. School supports it through activity, practical work and teaching about health.
points: Physical education, games, sport and dance develop gross motor skills (large body movements) such as running, jumping, balance and co-ordination, as well as strength, fitness and general body development.

Practical subjects such as Home Economics, Art, Construction Studies, Engineering and Science develop fine motor skills (small, precise hand movements), manual dexterity and hand-eye coordination. In early years, play with building blocks, jigsaws, drawing and writing does the same.
Regular physical activity strengthens muscles and bones and builds cardiovascular fitness (a healthy heart and lungs).
Lessons on nutrition, hygiene, safety and health (in SPHE, Home Economics and PE) give pupils the knowledge to look after their physical health.
Physical education and school sport can establish exercise habits that a person keeps into adult life, so the benefit lasts beyond school.
notes.tip: In a discussion of the development of the individual, give at least two specific physical points and name a subject or activity as the example, such as manual dexterity through practical subjects. A past paper on social and physical development expected physical development through PE, practical work and extracurricular activities.

notes.b: Emotional development is learning to understand and manage feelings and to get on with other people. School gives children many situations that call for this.
points: Starting school moves a child towards emotional independence from parents, because they meet other adults and peers outside the home, cope with separation and learn to depend on themselves.
Group work and class discussion develop empathy, the ability to understand and respond to the feelings of others, and help pupils express their own feelings appropriately.
Education helps a young person form healthy relationships and friendships.
Coping with success and failure in tests, sport, performances and tasks builds resilience (the ability to recover from setbacks), confidence, self-esteem and maturity.
Praise and encouragement from teachers strengthen self-worth.

The Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE) programme teaches emotional literacy (recognising and naming feelings), relationships, coping skills and personal safety. It continues into senior cycle as a non-exam programme.
Guidance counsellors and pastoral care (support for pupils' wellbeing) give extra help.
notes.tip: Pair each point with an example, such as empathy developed through group work. Marks go for one specific point plus an example for each area of development.

notes.b: Moral development is learning the difference between right and wrong and acting on it. School teaches this through its rules, its subjects and the people in it.
points: The ethos of a school sets out its values and the behaviour it expects from pupils.
School rules, sanctions and rewards teach pupils to distinguish right from wrong, fairness and accountability for their actions, because actions have consequences they must accept.
Religious education and SPHE address moral questions such as honesty, fairness, respect and tolerance, and subjects such as History and English raise the same questions.
Moral development is also shaped by teachers as role models and by the example of the peer group.
Pupils learn to respect the rights, property and opinions of others and to accept responsibility, so becoming responsible citizens.
notes.tip: Link moral development to school rules and ethos for right and wrong. Give a specific point and an example, such as rules and sanctions teaching accountability.

notes.b: Intellectual development is the growth of knowledge and thinking skills. A school's curriculum and assessment are built to promote it.
points: A broad curriculum develops literacy, numeracy, languages, scientific reasoning, creativity and artistic skills, and builds knowledge across many subjects.
Subjects that require analysis, argument and problem solving, and research, develop critical thinking and the ability to apply knowledge.
Concentration and memory are trained through homework, revision and classroom tasks, because they require pupils to practise focusing and recalling.
Examinations and continuous assessment (work marked throughout the year) measure learning and progress, and give motivation, goals and a sense of achievement.
Competition in class, sport, quizzes and extra-curricular activities challenges students to extend their abilities.
Education also builds curiosity and a habit of lifelong learning.
notes.tip: For a discussion of the purpose of education for the individual, give the four areas in the order physical, emotional, moral, intellectual, each with at least two specific points and a named subject or activity, such as thinking skills through problem-solving subjects. Do not add social development as a fifth area; put social points under socialisation.

notes.b: Most people spend much of their lives working, and school is where the groundwork is laid. Education gives skills, qualifications and habits that employers look for.
points: Literacy, numeracy, communication and computer or ICT skills are basic skills that employers expect in almost every job.

Qualifications such as Junior Cycle and the Leaving Certificate, and Post Leaving Certificate, further education and third-level awards, show employers what a person has learned and open doors to jobs and higher-paid work.
Higher levels of education are linked with better employment prospects.

Punctuality, good attendance, respect for authority, reliability, trustworthiness, responsibility, self-discipline and teamwork are taught through daily school routines and group tasks. Social skills are learned by working with others.

Work experience (in Transition Year, the Leaving Certificate Vocational Programme (LCVP) and the Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA)), career guidance and subjects chosen for a career help students connect school with the world of work.
Vocational and practical subjects such as Business Studies teach skills used directly in employment.

Education matters more as industry changes, because technology and a service-based economy raise the education required for employment. It also prepares people to retrain throughout their working life.
notes.tip: When asked for ways education prepares a young person for work, draw on basic skills, ICT, qualities such as respect for authority, punctuality, trustworthiness, responsibility and self-discipline, social skills and work experience. A short question may ask for three work-related qualities taught in school.

keyTerms.definition: The lifelong process by which a person learns the norms, values and behaviour of their society.
Learning that is planned and delivered through the timetable, curriculum and classroom rules.
The unplanned learning that pupils gain from school routines, peer groups and the school's ethos.
The values, beliefs and expectations that shape the character and behaviour of a school community.
Skills that use large muscle groups, such as running, jumping and balance.
Skills that use small, precise movements of the hands and fingers, such as writing or cutting.
The ability to understand and respond to the feelings and experiences of another person.
The ability to recover from setbacks and continue working towards a goal.
Education that prepares a person for a particular trade, occupation or area of employment.

factCards.term: Two sources of unplanned learning in school
factCards.definition: Peer groups and playground behaviour, and the school's routines and ethos.

factCards.term: Four aspects of a child's development that education supports
factCards.definition: Physical, emotional, moral and intellectual development.

factCards.term: Three work-related attributes taught through school routines
factCards.definition: Punctuality, reliability and responsibility, with self-discipline and teamwork also developed in group tasks.

factCards.term: Two basic skills employers expect in almost every job
Subject area that develops fine motor skills
factCards.definition: Practical subjects such as Home Economics, Art, Construction Studies and Science, which build manual dexterity.

factCards.term: Programme that teaches emotional literacy and personal safety

questions.prompt: Outline three ways in which a school prepares a student for working life.
questions.model: Any three, one mark for each developed point, to a maximum of six: basic literacy and numeracy skills that employers require; recognised qualifications that show employers what a student has achieved; work-related attributes such as punctuality, reliability, teamwork and self-discipline developed through school routines; career guidance and work experience that link subjects to employment; vocational subjects that teach practical skills used in specific jobs.

questions.prompt: Discuss how education contributes to a child's social development and to their preparation for work.
questions.model: Social development: formal socialisation through the timetable, curriculum and classroom rules, which teach respect for authority, punctuality and following instructions; informal socialisation through the hidden curriculum, peer groups and school ethos; first experience of a group outside the family, where children learn to share, take turns and cooperate; transmission of the culture, language and civic values of society; learning responsibility and respect for the rights of others. Preparation for work: literacy and numeracy as basic employment skills; qualifications such as the Junior Certificate, Leaving Certificate and Post Leaving Certificate courses that certify learning to employers; work-related attributes such as teamwork, reliability, responsibility and self-discipline developed through daily routines and group tasks; career guidance and work experience that connect school subjects with working life; vocational subjects that teach practical skills for particular jobs.
